reading.body:
Virginia's 2026 legislative session treated data centers as an infrastructure problem, not just a technology one, with bills on their power, water, noise, zoning, and tax treatment.

The volume is the story. Of 152 tracked bills, a large share touch data centers directly: cost recovery for serving them, retail sales tax exemptions, water use reporting, emergency generator limits, site assessment and sound profiles, local zoning and a proposed moratorium, land conservation taxes, and rainwater harvesting. The same session produced a parallel stack of AI bills covering chatbots and minors, employment decision systems, law enforcement inventories, health carrier disclosures, and school instruction. Two frameworks recur across both stacks: one creating an independent verification role for AI systems, another establishing a technology governance program. The pattern is a state writing rules for the physical plant and the software at the same time, which is what a jurisdiction hosting a concentration of compute has to do.

For AI specifically, the binding items are the ones about power and siting. Bills on electric utility cost allocation for data center customers, on integrated resource plans, on natural gas fuel cells and Tier 2 emergency generators, and on water consumption all address whether the load can be served and where it can sit. That is the constraint that determines how much compute Virginia can host, and the legislation treats it as a utility and land use question rather than an AI question. The tax bills matter for the same reason: exemptions, delayed effective dates, and new revenue classifications change the cost of building there.

The data does not say which bills passed, only that they were introduced and when. It records no votes, no committee outcomes, no signing or veto. The news items are four dated headlines about governors and federal oversight, three of them about figures outside Virginia's legislature, and they do not establish what any bill became. Nothing here measures actual data center load, water draw, or emissions, so the scale of the problem the bills respond to is asserted by their titles alone.

The bill stack splits into two clocks. The AI bills cluster in January, with the chatbot, employment, law enforcement, and verification framework titles all appearing between January 12 and January 22. The data center bills run later and longer, from the December 30 tax bill through the April 12 batch on water, sound, and zoning. A legislature writes the software rules first because they are cheap and abstract, then spends the spring on the land and power rules because those require utility commissions, localities, and revenue estimates.

The duplication is the mechanism worth noticing. Nearly every substantive data center idea appears twice, once as an HB and once as an SB: cost recovery for data center customers, retail sales tax exemptions, water use reporting, site assessment and sound profiles, distributed energy resources task forces, small portable solar regulation, integrated resource plans, emergency generator limits, land conservation taxes, rainwater harvesting. Paired introductions mean the same policy is moving through both chambers in parallel rather than one chamber leading. For a reader tracking whether Virginia will actually constrain compute, the pair is the unit to watch, not the individual bill.

The tax titles carry the most consequence per word. Exemptions for data centers, a delayed effective date on one, a new classification for major energy consumer equipment, a data center land conservation tax, and a local composite index change that routes data center revenue into school funding all appear in the same session. Each one moves the cost of siting compute in the state, and they move it in different directions. The data records only that they were introduced.

What did Virginia's 2026 session actually do about data centers?
The data records 152 tracked bills with titles and introduction dates, and a substantial share concern data centers, their power, water, noise, zoning, and taxes. It does not record passage, votes, or outcomes, so the session's actual effect cannot be determined from this page.

Which Virginia AI bills are most relevant to compute scaling?
The ones tied to power and siting: electric utility cost recovery for data center customers, integrated resource plans, natural gas fuel cells, Tier 2 emergency generator limits, and water consumption reporting. These determine whether load can be served and where facilities can sit. The chatbot, employment, and school instruction bills regulate uses of AI rather than the capacity to run it.

Why are there two bills with the same title?
Virginia introduces companion bills in the House and Senate, so the same policy appears as an HB and an SB. Cost recovery, sales tax exemptions, water reporting, site assessment, and the distributed energy resources task force all appear in pairs. The pair, not the single bill, is the meaningful unit.

Did any of these bills pass?
The data does not say. It contains bill numbers, titles, LegiScan URLs, and introduction dates, with no votes, committee actions, or signing records. The most recent bill date is June 28, 2026, and the most recent news item is October 2, 2026, but neither establishes an outcome.

What do the four news items tell us about Virginia's legislature?
Three concern figures outside it: a bipartisan governors group formed by Wes Moore and two items on Spanberger pressing for federal AI oversight. One, dated September 18, 2026, covers a state accountability framework for data centers and an AI task force. None reports legislative action on the bills listed.

How much power and water do Virginia data centers actually use?
The data does not contain load, consumption, or emissions figures. The bills reference water use consumption, waste heat, and generator emissions, but only as subjects of reporting requirements. The scale of the underlying problem is not measured anywhere in this dataset.
